result.rationale: The diff line `if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` in app/assets/javascripts/embed.js confirms the origin check is substring containment, not origin equality. Any e.origin that appears anywhere in discourseUrl (e.g., a prefix like 'https://for') passes, so the resize-message validation does not bind messages to the Discourse origin. The described mechanism is directly verifiable in the diff and constitutes a real defect in the intended security check.

judged_text: The postMessage origin check `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` is a substring containment test, not an origin equality test, so any origin that appears anywhere inside discourseUrl passes. A hostile embedding page whose origin is a substring of discourseUrl (trivially, any page when discourseUrl is short or when e.origin is a prefix like 'https://for') can post forged {type:'discourse-resize'} messages that control the iframe's rendered height — the boundary check the code exists to enforce does not actually bind the message to the Discourse origin.

A hostile embedding page whose origin is a substring of discourseUrl (trivially, any page when discourseUrl is short or when e.origin is a prefix like 'https://for') can post forged {type:'discourse-resize'} messages that control the iframe's rendered height — the boundary check the code exists to enforce does not actually bind the message to the Discourse origin.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/assets/javascripts/embed.js`, the message handler validates origin with `if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }`, which is a substring containment check rather than an equality check against the expected Discourse origin. This means a different (attacker-controlled) origin that happens to be a substring of `discourseUrl` would be accepted and could send forged `{type: 'discourse-resize'}` messages to control `iframe.height`.
